title: An optimal quantum strategy for the 2-hat game
authors: Georgios Baziotis; Sang-Jun Park; Sang-Gyun Youn
methods_basis: Based on the linked paper version. Derivations marked as editorial, and suggested uses in other problems, are editorial guidance rather than results of the paper.
problem: In the two-player hat game each player sees the other's random hat colour and must guess their own colour or pass; the team wins if someone guesses and nobody guesses wrong. Classically the best is \(1/2\). A strategy built for the stricter Feige game already showed that entanglement helps, reaching \(109/192\approx0.5677\), but the true quantum optimum, and whether infinite-dimensional commuting-operator strategies could beat finite-dimensional ones, were unknown.
result: The quantum and commuting-operator values coincide: \[\omega_{\mathrm q}(H_2)=\omega_{\mathrm{qc}}(H_2)=\frac{15+\sqrt{33}}{36}\approx0.5762.\] The value is attained by a non-maximally entangled pair of qutrits with rank-one projective measurements, and a matching upper bound comes from an exact sum-of-squares certificate. The no-signalling value is \(2/3\), and for \(n\) players no-signalling strategies win with probability at most \(n/(n+1)\), so for \(n=2^m-1\) nothing beats the classical Hamming-code strategy.
significance: It is one of few nonlocal games whose quantum value is known in closed form with an irrational optimum, and the proof shows how a symmetry group shrinks the certificate search enough to make it exact. It also settles the hat game's place in the hierarchy \(1/2<0.5762<2/3\) and rules out any advantage, quantum or even no-signalling, for the infinitely many player numbers where perfect Hamming codes exist.
limitations: The upper bound rests on a numerically found certificate (five positive semidefinite blocks) that the authors verify by exact calculation; it is specific to two players. Whether four or more players gain anything from entanglement is left open; for \(n=4\) the bounds are only \(3/4\le\omega_{\mathrm q}\le4/5\). The authors used OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra to find candidate strategy parameters and candidate certificate blocks, which they then simplified and verified.
summary_basis: Description based on the full arXiv HTML of v1, read 2026-11-12: the introduction and AI disclosure, Sections 2–5 (strategy, Bell operator, D8 symmetry reduction, certificate statement, no-signalling bound). The appendices with the explicit certificate blocks were not checked entry by entry. The strategy's value, the no-signalling and classical values, and the upper bound (by an independent level-1+AB NPA computation) were checked numerically.
description: Alice and Bob each wear a hat whose colour is an independent fair bit; Alice sees Bob's colour \(y\), Bob sees Alice's colour \(x\), and each answers \(0\), \(1\) or pass. With no communication, the team wins on the outputs \((x,\text{pass})\), \((\text{pass},y)\) and \((x,y)\). Any fixed strategy loses half the time: one player always guessing gets exactly \(1/2\), and nothing classical does better.

The question is the exact value of this two-input, three-output game when the players share entanglement, both in the finite-dimensional tensor-product model and in the commuting-operator model, where the two could in principle differ.

The optimal strategy shares \(\ket\Omega=\alpha(\ket{00}+\ket{11}+t\ket{22})\) with \(t=\sqrt{(7-\sqrt{33})/2}\approx0.785\), and each player measures in one of two real orthonormal bases of \(\mathbb C^3\). On every hat configuration, the two single-guess events each occur with probability \((55+9\sqrt{33})/396\approx0.269\) and the double correct guess with \((55-7\sqrt{33})/396\approx0.037\); summed, they give \((15+\sqrt{33})/36\). For the upper bound the authors write \(\lambda I-\Phi\), where \(\Phi\) is the game's Bell operator, as \(\mathbf w^*Z\mathbf w\) with \(Z\succeq0\) over 25 operator words (the identity, single projectors, and Alice–Bob products), which shows no commuting-operator strategy exceeds \(\lambda\).

A simple counting argument gives the no-signalling bound \(n/(n+1)\) for \(n\) players, and an explicit correlation reaches \(2/3\) for two. Open questions are whether entanglement helps at \(n=4\), the first player number between Hamming-code cases, and how the gap between quantum and no-signalling values behaves for larger \(n\).

methods.explanation: Proving that no strategy, of any dimension, beats a value needs an operator inequality \(\Phi\le\lambda I\) valid in the universal algebra of commuting measurements. The authors search for it as a positive semidefinite Gram matrix and use the game's symmetries to make the search small enough to solve exactly.
math: Eliminate the pass projectors with \(\sum_aM^y_a=I\), so the Bell operator involves only the guess projectors \(M^y_a,N^x_b\). If \[\lambda I-\Phi=\sum_{i,j}z_{ij}\,w_i^*w_j,\qquad Z=(z_{ij})\succeq0,\] then factoring \(Z=R^TR\) writes \(\lambda I-\Phi\) as a sum of squares \(\sum_kc_k^*c_k\), whose expectation in any state is nonnegative. Matching coefficients of each reduced word turns this into linear equations on \(Z\).

Swapping colours for one player, swapping the players, and their compositions are automorphisms that fix \(\Phi\) and permute the 25 words; they generate the dihedral group \(D_8\). Averaging any certificate over the group gives another certificate, so \(Z\) can be taken invariant, and Schur's lemma then block-diagonalizes it into blocks of sizes 5, 2, 4, 2 and 6 (the last twice). That cuts the unknowns from 325 to 52, few enough to guess closed forms from numerics and verify them exactly.

Editorial check: the moment-matrix relaxation dual to this certificate (NPA level 1+AB over the same 25 words) solved numerically gives \(0.576238\), equal to \((15+\sqrt{33})/36\) to solver precision.
methods.transfer: For any nonlocal game with a symmetry group acting on questions and answers, average the SDP certificate over the group and block-diagonalize by irreducible representations before trying to make it exact; the reduction often turns a numerical bound into a provable one.

methods.technique: Union bound with flipped configurations for no-signalling games
methods.explanation: The \(n/(n+1)\) bound holds for every strategy that cannot signal, so it bounds quantum strategies without any operator algebra. It uses only the fact that a player's own output cannot depend on their own hat, which they do not see.
math: Let \(s(x)\) be the winning probability on configuration \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) and \(x^{(i)}\) the configuration with bit \(i\) flipped. A win needs a correct guess, so \(s(x)\le\sum_ip_i(x_i)\). Player \(i\) sees the same input on \(x\) and \(x^{(i)}\), so guessing \(x_i\) has the same probability on both, and on \(x^{(i)}\) that guess is wrong: \(p_i(x_i)\le1-s(x^{(i)})\). Hence \[s(x)+\sum_{i=1}^ns(x^{(i)})\le n.\]

Each flip \(x\mapsto x^{(i)}\) is a bijection, so summing over all \(x\) gives \((n+1)\sum_xs(x)\le n2^n\), i.e. an average winning probability at most \(n/(n+1)\). For two players the correlation that outputs \((x,\text{pass})\), \((\text{pass},y)\) or \((1-x,1-y)\) with probability \(1/3\) each has uniform marginals, so it is no-signalling, and it wins with probability \(2/3\). Editorial check: a linear program over all no-signalling correlations returns \(2/3\).
methods.transfer: In guessing games where a player's input omits exactly the variable they must guess, pair each configuration with its flips; the no-signalling constraint converts every correct guess into a forced loss elsewhere, which gives quick upper bounds valid for all physical theories.
